title: Finite normalized models and their pure curve fibres
statement:
Let $k$ be a field, $S$ a normal integral projective finite-type $k$-scheme with $K=k(S)$, and $f:X\to S$ an H-projective morphism with $X$ integral of finite type over $k$. Suppose the geometric fibres of $f$ are pure of dimension one and its generic fibre is smooth and geometrically integral. Write $F=k(X)$. Let $L/F$ be a finite separable field extension and $E/K$ a finite separable subextension of $L/K$. Suppose the normalization of $X_K$ in $L$, with its induced $E$-structure, is a smooth projective geometrically integral $E$-curve $C$. Put $T=\operatorname{Nor}_E(S)$ and $Y=\operatorname{Nor}_L(X)$. Then $T$ is normal integral projective of finite type over $k$, with function field $E$, and $T\to S$ is finite surjective. The scheme $Y$ is normal integral of finite type over $k$, with function field $L$. The structural maps factor canonically as $Y\to X\times_ST\to X$. The first map is finite surjective, and $Y\to T$ is H-projective with all geometric fibres pure of dimension one and generic fibre $C$. The composite $Y\to X$ is finite. The hypotheses on $L,E,C$ hold in particular for a finite separable extension $E/K$ and $L=F\otimes_K E$: this tensor product is a field and $C=X_K\times_K E$. These constructions are functorial for compatible isomorphisms of the scheme and field data, including isomorphisms that act on $k$. In particular every compatible group action on $X,S,L,E$ extends uniquely to $Y,T$. If $U\subseteq S$ is open and $Z\to X_U$ is a finite dominant morphism with $Z$ normal integral and a specified $F$-embedding $k(Z)\hookrightarrow L$, then there is a unique $X_U$-morphism $Y_U\to Z$ inducing that embedding; this morphism is finite.

The notions used are [def-weil-field], [def-pc-integral-scheme], [def-weil-finite-type-morphism], [def-weil-finite-integral-morphism], [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms], [def-pc-geometrically-irreducible], [def-kun-projective], [def-sc-function-field], [def-pc-field-extension], [def-fin-normalization-extension], [def-pc-fibre-product], [def-weil-pure-dimension]. Normal means that every local ring is an integrally closed domain. A finite separable extension is a finite-dimensional field extension whose elements have separable minimal polynomials. Group actions on schemes and fields may be nonfaithful and semilinear on the ground field.

proof.text: Apply the finite-normalization model theorem to $(X,F,L)$ and $(S,K,E)$. It gives normal integral finite-type schemes $Y,T$, their stated function fields, and finite surjective normalization maps; in particular $Y\to X$ is finite. Its open restriction and intermediate-model clauses give exactly the unique finite map $Y_U\to Z$ in the statement.

proof.text: Apply the normalized-base factorization theorem to $f,L,E$. Its hypotheses hold because the given generic fibre is geometrically integral. It supplies the canonical $g:Y\to T$, the finite surjection $Y\to X\times_ST$, the field $F\otimes_KE$, and the identification of the generic fibre of $g$ with the specified $C$. The last fibre is nonempty and pure one-dimensional by hypothesis. Apply the finite relative curve-factor theorem to $q,\nu,g$: it gives projectivity of $T/k$ and H-projectivity of $g$, and pure dimension one for every geometric fibre.

proof.text: For the special case of a finite separable constant extension $E/K$, first show directly that $L=F\otimes_KE$ is a field (step 2 cannot be invoked before such an $L$ is available). Choose a nonempty affine $\operatorname{Spec}D\subseteq X_K$. Since $X_K$ is geometrically integral, $X_K\times_KE$ is integral, so $D\otimes_KE$ is a domain; its localization at $D\setminus\{0\}$ is $F\otimes_KE$, a nonzero domain of finite dimension over $F$, hence a field (multiplication by a nonzero element is injective $F$-linear, hence bijective). It is finite separable over $F$: a finite separable extension has a primitive element with separable minimal polynomial $p$, and $L=F[t]/(p)$ is a field; the Bezout identity for $p,p\prime$ remains valid over $F$. The base change $X_K\times_KE$ is smooth of relative dimension one and projective, by smooth and projective base change, and geometrically integral by the definition. A smooth curve over a field is normal. The finite-algebra integrality theorem shows that its affine rings (finite modules because $E/K$ is finite) are integral over the affine rings of $X_K$ and have fraction field $L$. Conversely, an element of $L$ integral over an original affine ring is integral over its normal base-changed ring, and hence belongs to it. Thus this base change is exactly the normalization in $L$, yielding the stated $C$.

proof.text: For compatible isomorphisms of $X,S,L,E$, apply the semilinear functoriality assertion of the normalization model theorem to $Y$ and $T$. Their induced maps commute with $g$ by the uniqueness clause of the normalized-base factorization theorem: both composites have the same map over $S$ and the same embedding of $E$ into $L$. Identity and composition compatibility give the action laws for each compatible group action, with uniqueness supplied by the same normalization theorem.
